claims.claim: Didymus the Blind was a Christian theologian who headed the catechetical school of Alexandria in the fourth century (c. 313–398).
He was born in Alexandria, Egypt, and lost his eyesight at about four years old, remaining a layman all his life.
Didymus wrote a line‑by‑line commentary on the Book of Job (Commentarii in Job) that covers the first sixteen chapters of the Septuagint version of Job.
It was produced at a time when Christianity and Rabbinic Judaism were developing distinct interpretive traditions, making its LXX‑based exegesis especially significant.
Didymus’s association with Origen led to his works being condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, after which they were no longer copied in the Middle Ages.
The surviving text of the Job commentary is preserved in a group of papyrus codices discovered in 1941 at a munitions dump near Tura, Egypt.
The Tura papyri containing the commentary are now housed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and have been edited and published in a four‑volume critical Greek edition by Hagedorn, Koenen and colleagues.
The commentary is one of the earliest line‑by‑line biblical commentaries from late antiquity that has survived, providing a valuable window into early Christian exegesis.

Modern scholars regard the work important for understanding early Christian responses to suffering and for its influence on later theological reflection, including contemporary interest in the Holocaust and other atrocities.
